chapter.name: Some Applications of Trigonometry
chapter.blurb: A student measuring a minar's height without a ladder, an electrician's ladder reaching a point below a pole's top, and a bridge's-eye view of a river's two banks all turn on the same idea: once the angle a line of sight makes with the horizontal is known, together with one length in the right triangle it forms, every other length in that triangle follows from a trigonometric ratio. The chapter names the angle of elevation (looking up) and the angle of depression (looking down), then works through heights and distances of increasing structural complexity: a single triangle, a triangle adjusted for the observer's own height or a broken pole, two triangles stacked on a shared base (a flagstaff on a building), two triangles from one elevated point to two ground points (a river's banks), and the same fixed height viewed from two positions or two moments, whose difference gives a distance travelled or a time taken.

scope_in.item: Define the line of sight, the angle of elevation and the angle of depression, and identify them correctly in a diagram or word problem

Understand that, because the horizontals at two different heights are parallel lines, the angle of elevation of a higher point measured from a lower point equals the angle of depression of that lower point measured from the higher point (alternate angles)

Identify the right triangle in a heights-and-distances word problem (the vertical height, the horizontal distance, and the hypotenuse formed by the line of sight or a taut rope/wire/ladder/string), and choose the trigonometric ratio (or its reciprocal) connecting the two known/unknown quantities
Solve for an unknown height or distance in a single right triangle using tan or cot, when the height and the horizontal distance are the two lengths involved
Solve for an unknown length (the hypotenuse, or a height/distance given the hypotenuse) in a single right triangle using sin or cos, for a taut rope, ladder or string
Account for the observer's own height (eye level) when the observer is not a point on the ground, by adding or subtracting it as appropriate
Solve problems involving a pole or tree that breaks and bends, where the standing stump and the fallen part form two sides of a right triangle, and the original height is their sum

Solve two-right-triangle problems where one object stands on top of another at the same horizontal distance (a flagstaff on a building, a statue on a pedestal, a tower on a building), finding the height of the upper part by subtracting

Solve two-right-triangle problems using two angles of depression from one elevated point to two ground-level points, adding the two horizontal distances when the points are on opposite sides and subtracting them when the points are on the same side

Solve problems where the same fixed-height object is observed from two different points or at two different times, subtracting the two horizontal distances to find the distance travelled or (given a time interval) the object's speed or the time for a further stage of the journey
Use the shadow-length-difference method: relate the height of an object to the difference between its shadow lengths at two different angles of elevation of the sun

scope_out.item: Proving trigonometric identities, or deriving/manipulating the trigonometric ratios themselves (such as sin^2 + cos^2 = 1)
scope_out.reason: The chapter opens by saying the student has already studied trigonometric ratios in the previous chapter and only applies the already-known ratios of 30, 45 and 60 degrees to real-life heights and distances; it develops no new ratio identities of its own (p. 133).

scope_out.item: Trigonometric ratios of angles other than 30, 45 and 60 degrees, or the use of trigonometric tables or a calculator for a non-standard angle
scope_out.reason: Every worked example and every exercise question in this chapter uses only the standard angles 30, 45 and 60 degrees; no other angle value appears anywhere in the chapter.

scope_out.item: Finding an unknown angle (using an inverse trigonometric ratio) from two known side lengths
scope_out.reason: In every example and exercise, the angle (30, 45 or 60 degrees) is always one of the given quantities and the problem always solves for a missing length; the chapter never asks the student to work out an unknown angle from given lengths.

scope_out.item: Bearings, compass directions, or any problem where the object and the observer(s) are not in one vertical plane
scope_out.reason: Every example and exercise problem in this chapter is confined to a single vertical plane containing the object and the observer(s) -- towers, buildings, rivers and roads viewed face-on; no three-dimensional or compass-direction setup appears.

scope_out.item: The sine rule, the cosine rule, or any method for a triangle that is not right-angled
scope_out.reason: Every triangle formed in this chapter is a right triangle, created because the objects (towers, poles, buildings) are assumed exactly vertical and the ground exactly horizontal (p. 133); no oblique-triangle method is used or needed.

scope_out.item: Finding the area or perimeter of the right triangle formed in a heights-and-distances problem
scope_out.reason: Every example and exercise asks only for a height, a distance, a length (such as a ladder or rope) or a time; none asks for the area or perimeter of the triangle formed.

concepts.name: Line of sight, angle of elevation and angle of depression
concepts.description: The line of sight from an observer's eye to the point being viewed; the angle of elevation (line of sight above the horizontal, looking up) and the angle of depression (line of sight below the horizontal, looking down); and the fact that, because the horizontals at two different heights are parallel, the angle of elevation of a higher point from a lower point equals the angle of depression of that lower point from the higher point.
concepts.idea: The angle of elevation or depression is always measured from the horizontal at the observer's own eye, never from the vertical or from the line joining the two objects themselves.
concepts.rule: Line of sight: the line from the observer's eye to the point on the object viewed. Angle of elevation: the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal, when the viewed point is above the horizontal level (raising the head to look). Angle of depression: the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal, when the viewed point is below the horizontal level (lowering the head to look). Since the horizontals at any two heights are parallel lines, and the line of sight is a transversal cutting them, the angle of elevation of a higher point measured from a lower point equals the angle of depression of that lower point measured from the higher point (alternate angles).
concepts.example: A student looking up at the top of a minar: the angle her line of sight makes with the horizontal is the angle of elevation (Fig. 9.1, p. 133). A girl sitting on a balcony looking down at a flower pot on a step below: the angle formed is the angle of depression (Fig. 9.3, p. 134).

questions.q: The line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point on the object being viewed is called the
questions.a: line of sight

questions.q: When the point being viewed is above the horizontal level, the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal is called the
questions.a: angle of elevation

questions.q: When the point being viewed is below the horizontal level, the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal is called the angle of ____.
questions.a: depression

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT correct about the angle of elevation and the angle of depression?
questions.a: The angle of elevation of a point equals the ratio height/distance itself, rather than being the angle whose tangent gives that ratio
o: The angle of elevation of a point equals the ratio height/distance itself, rather than being the angle whose tangent gives that ratio
Both angles are measured from the horizontal, never from the vertical
The angle of elevation is used when we raise our head to look at a point above the horizontal level
The angle of depression is used when we lower our head to look at a point below the horizontal level

questions.q: In Fig. 9.1 of the chapter, a student looks up at the top of a minar. Which angle does the line from her eye to the top of the minar make with the horizontal?
questions.a: angle of elevation

questions.q: A girl sitting on a balcony looks down at a flower pot on a step below. The angle formed with the horizontal by her line of sight to the flower pot is called the
questions.a: angle of depression

questions.q: Why could the very same angle be called an angle of elevation for one observer and an angle of depression for another?
questions.a: Because it depends on whether the horizontal at the observer's own eye is below the object (elevation) or above the object (depression)
o: Because it depends on whether the horizontal at the observer's own eye is below the object (elevation) or above the object (depression)
Because elevation and depression are always different angles for the same two points
Because the object physically moves between the two viewings
Because one observer is always taller than the other

questions.q: A man standing at the top of a tower looks down at a car on the road below, and the angle of depression is 40 degrees. What is the angle of elevation of the man, as seen from the car?
questions.a: 40 degrees

questions.q: Explain, using the fact that the horizontal at a low point and the horizontal at a high point are parallel lines, why the angle of elevation of the top of a tower observed from a point on the ground equals the angle of depression of that ground point observed from the top of the tower.
questions.a: The two horizontal lines (one at the ground point, one at the top of the tower) are parallel, and the line of sight joining the two points is a transversal cutting both; the angle of elevation at the ground point and the angle of depression at the top are alternate angles formed by this transversal, so they are equal.
s: States that the two horizontals are parallel and the line of sight is a transversal
Concludes the two angles are equal because they are alternate angles

questions.q: A student stands on level ground and looks up at a bird sitting on a wall higher than her eyes. The angle her line of sight makes with the horizontal is
questions.a: an angle of elevation, since the bird is above the horizontal level of her eyes
o: an angle of elevation, since the bird is above the horizontal level of her eyes
an angle of depression, since the bird is far away
a right angle, since the wall is vertical
undefined, since a bird is not a fixed point

questions.q: A pilot flying at a height looks down at an airport on the ground. The angle her line of sight makes with the horizontal at her eye is called the angle of ____.
questions.a: depression

questions.q: From the top of a cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is 25 degrees. As the boat moves further away from the foot of the cliff, staying on the same straight line, what happens to this angle of depression?
questions.a: It decreases
o: It becomes an angle of elevation

questions.q: A girl of height 1.4 m stands so that her eye level is 1.3 m above the ground, and looks up at a balloon. State whether the vertical distance she should use in her trigonometric ratio is measured from her feet or from her eye level, and why.
questions.a: From her eye level, because the angle of elevation is defined using the horizontal at the observer's eye, so the relevant vertical distance is from her eye to the balloon, not from the ground to the balloon.
s: States the vertical distance must be measured from eye level, not the ground
Gives the reason: the angle of elevation/depression is always defined at the observer's eye

questions.q: Two horizontal lines are drawn, one through a point A at ground level and one through a point P at the top of a tower directly above a point on the ground. A line of sight joins A and P. Name the two angles formed at A and at P by this line of sight with the respective horizontals, and state the relationship between them.
questions.a: At A, the angle formed is the angle of elevation of P from A; at P, the angle formed is the angle of depression of A from P. Since the two horizontals are parallel, these two angles are equal (alternate angles).
s: Correctly names both angles (elevation at A, depression at P)
States they are equal, since alternate angles on parallel horizontals

questions.q: A boy stands at point A on the ground and looks up at a flag at the top of a pole at an angle of elevation of 35 degrees. His friend stands right at the top of the same pole and looks down at the boy. (i) Name the angle her line of sight makes with the horizontal. (ii) State its measure, giving a reason. (iii) Explain in one line why this equality would fail if the two horizontals were not parallel.
questions.a: (i) Angle of depression. (ii) 35 degrees, because the two horizontals (at A and at the top of the pole) are parallel, and the line of sight is a transversal, making the angle of elevation at A and the angle of depression at the top alternate angles, hence equal. (iii) If the two horizontals were not parallel, the transversal would not create equal alternate angles, so the two angles could differ.
s: Names the angle correctly as angle of depression
States it equals 35 degrees with the alternate-angles reason
Explains that non-parallel horizontals would break the equality

questions.q: Assertion (A): The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground equals the angle of depression of that point from the top of the tower. Reason (R): The horizontal line at the ground point and the horizontal line at the top of the tower are parallel, and the line of sight is a transversal, making the two angles alternate angles.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Consider these statements about angles of elevation and depression. (I) The angle of elevation is always measured from the horizontal at the observer's eye, not from the ground directly beneath the observer. (II) An angle of depression can only occur when the observer is standing on level ground. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Point B is on the ground at the foot of a tower, and point C is also on the ground, further away from the tower than B, both on the same straight line as the tower's foot. From the top of the tower, the angle of depression of B is 60 degrees and the angle of depression of C is 30 degrees. (i) Which of B or C is closer to the foot of the tower? Give a one-line reason using the general behaviour of the angle of depression with distance. (ii) Which angle, the one to B or the one to C, is larger? (iii) If the height of the tower were doubled while B and C stayed in the same places, would the angle of depression of B increase, decrease, or stay the same?
questions.a: (i) B is closer, because for a fixed tower height, a nearer point makes a larger angle of depression than a farther point. (ii) The angle to B (60 degrees) is larger. (iii) It would increase, since increasing the height while keeping the horizontal distance fixed increases the ratio height/distance, and hence the angle whose tangent is that ratio.
s: Identifies B as closer with a correct one-line reason
Correctly states the angle to B (60 degrees) is larger
Correctly states the angle of depression to B would increase if height doubles

questions.q: A classmate claims: 'The angle of elevation and the angle of depression between the same two points are always different, because one is called elevation and the other is called depression.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is false. The two angles are equal in size (by alternate angles on the parallel horizontals); only the name differs, depending on which of the two points is doing the observing -- elevation when looking up, depression when looking down at the other point -- not the numerical measure of the angle.
s: States the claim is false
Explains the two angles have equal measure, only the name differs by which point is observing

questions.q: Describe a real-life situation, different from any example in this chapter, in which you would measure an angle of depression, and a second real-life situation in which you would measure an angle of elevation. For each, name the observer, the object viewed, and state whether the observer's line of sight goes up or down from the horizontal.
questions.a: Sample: (1) Angle of depression -- a lifeguard sitting on a raised chair looks down at a swimmer in the water; the line of sight goes down from the horizontal at the lifeguard's eyes. (2) Angle of elevation -- a person standing at the base of a hill looks up at a paraglider in the sky; the line of sight goes up from the horizontal at the person's eyes. (Any two genuine, distinct, correctly labelled real-life situations are acceptable.)
s: Gives a valid angle-of-depression scenario with observer, object and downward line of sight correctly identified
Gives a valid angle-of-elevation scenario with observer, object and upward line of sight correctly identified
Both scenarios are original (not copied from the chapter's own examples/exercises) and internally consistent

concepts.name: Finding a height or distance using one trig ratio in a single right triangle
concepts.description: Setting up the single right triangle formed by a vertical object, the horizontal ground, and the line of sight (or a taut rope, wire, ladder or string running from the top of the object to a point on the ground), and choosing tan (or cot) when height and horizontal distance are the two lengths involved, or sin/cos when the hypotenuse (the slant length) is one of the two lengths involved.
concepts.idea: In a right triangle formed by a vertical height, a horizontal distance and a slant line of sight (or rope/ladder/string), the given angle tells you directly which trigonometric ratio connects the two lengths you know and want.
concepts.rule: If height and horizontal distance are the two lengths involved, use tan(angle) = height / distance (or cot(angle) = distance / height). If the hypotenuse (a rope, ladder or string) and the height are involved, use sin(angle) = height / hypotenuse. If the hypotenuse and the horizontal distance are involved, use cos(angle) = distance / hypotenuse.
concepts.example: A tower stands on ground level; from a point 15 m from its foot, the angle of elevation of its top is 60 degrees. tan 60 degrees = height / 15, giving height = 15 root 3 m (Example 1, p. 135).

questions.q: In a right triangle formed to find the height of a tower, if the angle of elevation and the horizontal distance from the tower are known, which trigonometric ratio directly relates height and distance?
questions.a: tan (or cot)

questions.q: In a right triangle, tan(angle) is defined as
questions.a: opposite side / adjacent side

questions.q: If a rope of fixed length is stretched from the top of a pole to a point on the ground, and the angle it makes with the ground is known, the ratio connecting the height of the pole and the length of the rope (its hypotenuse) is the ____ of the angle.
questions.a: sine

questions.q: In a single right triangle used to find a height or distance, which of the following is NOT a correct way to choose the trigonometric ratio?
questions.a: Always subtract the angle of depression from the angle of elevation before choosing a ratio, since the two angles are alternate angles of the same triangle
o: Always subtract the angle of depression from the angle of elevation before choosing a ratio, since the two angles are alternate angles of the same triangle
Use tan(angle) = height / horizontal distance when both the height and the horizontal distance are involved
Use sin(angle) = height / hypotenuse when the height and a slant length are involved
Use cos(angle) = horizontal distance / hypotenuse when the horizontal distance and a slant length are involved

questions.q: A tower stands on level ground. From a point 20 m from its foot, the angle of elevation of its top is measured. Which two lengths does tan(angle) directly relate here?
questions.a: the height of the tower and the 20 m distance
o: the height of the tower and the 20 m distance
the height of the tower and the line of sight length
the 20 m distance and the line of sight length
none of these, since tan cannot be used here

questions.q: A kite string is tied to a point on the ground and makes an angle with the ground. Why is sin (not tan) the natural first choice if the height of the kite and the length of the string are the two quantities of interest?
questions.a: Because sin(angle) = opposite/hypotenuse directly connects the height (opposite side) and the string length (hypotenuse)
o: Because sin(angle) = opposite/hypotenuse directly connects the height (opposite side) and the string length (hypotenuse)
Because tan is only defined for angles less than 45 degrees
Because sin always gives a whole number answer
Because the string is horizontal, not slanted

questions.q: In a right triangle with the right angle at the foot of a vertical tower, the side opposite the angle of elevation measured at the ground point is
questions.a: the height of the tower
o: the horizontal distance from the tower

questions.q: A vertical pole and the horizontal ground it stands on meet at a right angle. From a ground point, the angle of elevation to the top of the pole is given, together with the horizontal distance. Which equation correctly finds the height h of the pole?
questions.a: h = distance x tan(angle)

questions.q: A tower stands on level ground. From a point 25 m away from its foot, the angle of elevation of its top is 45 degrees. Find the height of the tower, showing the trigonometric equation you use.
questions.a: tan 45 degrees = h/25, so 1 = h/25, giving h = 25 m.
s: Sets up tan 45 degrees = h/25 correctly
Solves to get h = 25 m

questions.q: From a point on the ground 10 root 3 m away from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of the top is 30 degrees. The height of the tower is
A tower is 10 m high. From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation of its top is 45 degrees. The distance of the point from the foot of the tower is ____ m.
A ladder rests against a wall so that the foot of the ladder is 6 m from the wall and the ladder makes an angle of 60 degrees with the ground. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
questions.a: 6 root 3 m

questions.q: A circus artist climbs a rope tightly stretched from the top of a vertical pole to a point on the ground 15 m from the foot of the pole. If the rope makes an angle of 30 degrees with the ground, find the length of the rope.
questions.a: cos 30 degrees = 15/L, so root 3/2 = 15/L, giving L = 30/root 3 = 10 root 3 m (approximately 17.32 m).
s: Sets up cos 30 degrees = 15/L correctly
Solves to get L = 10 root 3 m

questions.q: A string of a kite is 40 root 3 m long and makes an angle of 60 degrees with the level ground. Find the height of the kite above the ground, assuming the string is taut and straight.
questions.a: sin 60 degrees = h/(40 root 3), so root 3/2 = h/(40 root 3), giving h = 40 root 3 x root 3/2 = 60 m.
s: Sets up sin 60 degrees = h/(40 root 3) correctly
Solves to get h = 60 m

questions.q: A tower stands vertically on level ground. From a point on the ground 20 m from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 60 degrees. (i) Name the angle, the opposite side and the adjacent side of the right triangle you would use. (ii) Write the trigonometric equation connecting the height and the distance. (iii) Solve for the height of the tower, giving your answer as a surd and rounded to two decimal places (using root 3 = 1.732).
questions.a: (i) The right angle is at the foot of the tower; the angle of elevation 60 degrees is at the ground point; the opposite side is the height of the tower, the adjacent side is the 20 m distance. (ii) tan 60 degrees = height / 20. (iii) root 3 = height/20, so height = 20 root 3 m = 34.64 m (using root 3 = 1.732).
s: Correctly names the right angle, opposite side (height) and adjacent side (20 m distance)
Writes tan 60 degrees = height/20 correctly
Solves to get height = 20 root 3 m = 34.64 m

questions.q: Assertion (A): From a point 12 m from the foot of a tower, if the angle of elevation of the top is 45 degrees, the height of the tower is 6 m. Reason (R): tan 45 degrees = 1, so the height of the tower equals the horizontal distance from the point to the foot of the tower.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Consider these statements about using trigonometric ratios for heights and distances. (I) If the angle of elevation and the horizontal distance are known, the height can be found using tan(angle) = height / distance. (II) If the angle of elevation and the length of the line of sight (hypotenuse) are known, the height can be found using sin(angle) = height / hypotenuse. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Two right triangles are used to find the height of two different flagpoles, both using the tangent ratio. Flagpole P: distance 9 m, angle of elevation 60 degrees. Flagpole Q: distance 9 root 3 m, angle of elevation 30 degrees. (i) Find the height of flagpole P. (ii) Find the height of flagpole Q. (iii) State how the two heights compare.
questions.a: (i) Height of P: tan 60 degrees = h/9, so h = 9 root 3 m (about 15.59 m). (ii) Height of Q: tan 30 degrees = h/(9 root 3), so h = 9 root 3 / root 3 = 9 m. (iii) Flagpole P (9 root 3 m) is taller than flagpole Q (9 m).
s: Correctly finds height of P = 9 root 3 m
Correctly finds height of Q = 9 m
Correctly compares, stating P is taller

questions.q: A classmate says: 'To find the height of any tower, I can always use the tangent ratio, no matter what information is given.' Evaluate this claim using a situation where a taut wire's length (the hypotenuse) and the angle it makes with the ground are given, instead of the horizontal distance.
questions.a: The claim is false. If the length of a slanting wire (the hypotenuse) and the angle it makes with the ground are given, rather than the horizontal distance, the tangent ratio (which needs the adjacent side) is not directly usable; the sine ratio (opposite/hypotenuse) is the correct choice instead to find the height.
s: States the claim is false
Explains that with the hypotenuse (wire length) given instead of the distance, sine (not tangent) is the correct ratio for height

questions.q: Construct your own height-and-distance problem: choose a horizontal distance and an angle of elevation (using only 30, 45 or 60 degrees) so that the height comes out to be a whole number of metres. State your chosen distance and angle, write the trigonometric equation, and solve for the height.
questions.a: Sample: distance = 8 root 3 m, angle of elevation = 30 degrees. tan 30 degrees = h / (8 root 3), so h = 8 root 3 x (1/root 3) = 8 m. (Any distance-angle pair from 30, 45 or 60 degrees that gives a whole-number height, correctly solved, is acceptable.)
s: Chooses a valid distance and an angle from 30, 45 or 60 degrees
Writes the correct trigonometric equation for the chosen values
Solves correctly to obtain a whole-number height matching the chosen values

concepts.name: Accounting for the observer's eye-level height or a broken/partial vertical length
concepts.description: Word problems where the observer's eyes are above ground level (so the triangle's vertical leg is the object's height above eye level, not its full height, and the object's total height must be found by adding the observer's height back), or where only part of a vertical length is directly involved, such as a pole climbed part-way by a ladder, or a tree that breaks and whose upper part bends over to touch the ground, becoming the hypotenuse of a new right triangle with the remaining stump.
concepts.idea: When the observer's eyes are above the ground, or an object is only partly standing (with the rest bent over or climbed to), solve the triangle for the offset part first, then add or combine it with the known fixed part to answer the question actually asked.
concepts.rule: If the observer's height (eye level) is e and the total object height is H, the triangle gives (H - e) using tan(angle) = (H - e) / distance; then H = (H - e) + e. If a pole or tree of total height H breaks at a height h1 above the ground, and the broken upper part (length L, the hypotenuse) bends over to touch the ground at distance d from the foot, making angle theta with the ground: tan(theta) = h1 / d gives the stump height h1, and cos(theta) = d / L gives the broken length L; the original height = h1 + L.
concepts.example: An observer 1.5 m tall is 28.5 m from a chimney; the angle of elevation of its top from her eyes is 45 degrees, giving 28.5 m above her eye level, so the chimney's total height is 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m (Example 3, p. 137). A tree breaks and its top touches the ground 8 m from its foot at 30 degrees, giving a stump of 8 root 3 / 3 m and a broken part of 16 root 3 / 3 m, so the tree's original height was 8 root 3 m (Exercise 9.1, Q2, p. 141).

questions.q: When an observer's eyes are above the ground, the height of an object above the observer's eye level is found first, and then the observer's own height is
questions.a: added to it, to get the object's total height above the ground
o: added to it, to get the object's total height above the ground

questions.q: A tree breaks and the broken upper part bends over to touch the ground, still attached at the break point. In the right triangle this forms, the broken part (from the break point to where it touches the ground) is the
questions.a: hypotenuse
o: side opposite the angle at the ground
side adjacent to the angle at the ground

questions.q: If an observer of height e stands at a horizontal distance d from a tower of total height H, the vertical leg of the right triangle used with the angle of elevation is H minus ____.
questions.a: e

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a correct step when a tree of unknown original height breaks and its top touches the ground at a known distance, making a known angle with the ground?
questions.a: Find the tree's original height directly as the angle of depression of the break point from the point where the top touches the ground
o: Find the tree's original height directly as the angle of depression of the break point from the point where the top touches the ground
Use tan(angle) with the horizontal distance to find the height of the remaining standing stump
Use cos(angle) with the horizontal distance to find the length of the broken (fallen-over) part
Add the stump height and the length of the broken part to get the tree's original total height

questions.q: An observer 1.5 m tall stands 28.5 m from a chimney and finds the angle of elevation of its top, from her eyes, to be 45 degrees. Which length does solving the triangle directly give?
questions.a: the height of the chimney above the observer's eye level, not its full height above the ground
o: the height of the chimney above the observer's eye level, not its full height above the ground
the full height of the chimney above the ground directly
the distance from the chimney's foot to the observer's feet

questions.q: In the tree-breaking situation, why does the stump height plus the length of the fallen part give the tree's original height, rather than its height after breaking?
questions.a: Because before it broke, the tree was one straight vertical length equal to the stump plus the part that is now bent over
o: Because before it broke, the tree was one straight vertical length equal to the stump plus the part that is now bent over
Because trees always regrow to their original height
Because the stump and the fallen part are always equal in length
Because breaking a tree does not change its total length

questions.q: A 1.6 m tall girl looks up at a kite. To use the angle of elevation correctly in her right triangle, the vertical leg of the triangle should be measured from
questions.a: her eye level (approximately 1.6 m above the ground), not from the ground itself
o: her eye level (approximately 1.6 m above the ground), not from the ground itself
the ground directly below her feet
the midpoint between her feet and her eyes
the top of the kite only

questions.q: An electrician needs to reach a point 1.2 m below the top of a 6 m pole. What length should be used as the relevant vertical leg of her ladder's right triangle?
questions.a: 4.8 m (that is, 6 m minus 1.2 m)
o: 6 m, the full height of the pole
1.2 m, the distance below the top

concepts.name: Two heights from one point sharing a common horizontal distance (stacked objects)
concepts.description: Problems with two objects stacked vertically at the same horizontal position, such as a flagstaff on a building, a statue on a pedestal, or a transmission tower on a building, observed from a single ground point with two different angles of elevation to the two different tops; finding the length of the upper part, the height of the lower part, or the shared horizontal distance by solving two right triangles that share the same horizontal base.
concepts.idea: Both triangles share the same horizontal distance from the observation point to the foot of the combined structure; use a known height and its angle to find that shared distance, then use the second angle in the second triangle to find the remaining unknown, and add or subtract the two heights as the question requires.
concepts.rule: If the total height to the upper point is H2 and to the lower point is H1 (both measured from the ground, both directly above the same foot point, viewed from a ground point at distance d): tan(angle to upper) = H2 / d and tan(angle to lower) = H1 / d. If H1 (or d) is already known, solve one triangle for d (or H1) first, then use the other angle in the second triangle to find H2. The length of the object standing on top = H2 - H1.
concepts.example: A 10 m building has angle of elevation 30 degrees to its top from point P, giving distance AP = 10 root 3 m; a flagstaff on top makes the angle of elevation of its own top 45 degrees from the same point P, giving a flagstaff length of 10(root 3 - 1) m, about 7.32 m (Example 4, pp. 137-138).

concepts.name: Angles of depression from one height to two points on the ground
concepts.description: Problems where a single observation point at a known height looks down at two different points at ground level, on the same side or on opposite sides, such as a bridge over a river (opposite banks), or a lighthouse observing two ships (same side, one behind the other); solving two right triangles that share the same known vertical height for two separate horizontal distances, then adding them (opposite sides) or subtracting them (same side) to answer for the distance between the two ground points.
concepts.idea: Both triangles share the same known vertical height; use each angle of depression separately, converting it (by alternate angles) to the angle at the corresponding ground point, to get two horizontal distances, then add or subtract them depending on whether the two ground points lie on opposite sides or the same side of the point directly below the observer.
concepts.rule: With height h fixed: angle of depression theta1 to point 1 gives horizontal distance d1 = h / tan(theta1); angle of depression theta2 to point 2 gives d2 = h / tan(theta2). If the two points are on OPPOSITE sides of the foot of the height, the distance between them = d1 + d2. If they are on the SAME side (one further than the other), the distance between them = the larger distance minus the smaller distance.
concepts.example: From a bridge 3 m above the banks of a river, the angles of depression of the two opposite banks are 30 degrees and 45 degrees, giving distances of 3 root 3 m and 3 m, so the river's width = 3 root 3 + 3 = 3(root 3 + 1) m, about 8.2 m (Example 7, pp. 140-141).

concepts.name: Same object, two positions or two times: distance travelled or time taken
concepts.description: Problems where a single fixed-height object (a building, a balloon, a car) is viewed from two different ground positions, or at two different times as the observer or the object moves, giving two different angles of elevation or depression to the same fixed height; finding the distance between the two positions, or (given a time interval and uniform speed) the time for a further stage of the journey, by solving two right triangles that share the same height and subtracting the two horizontal distances.
concepts.idea: The object's height stays fixed throughout; only the angle changes as the horizontal distance changes, so solve two separate right triangles sharing that one height for the two horizontal distances, and subtract them to get the distance covered between the two observations.
concepts.rule: With height h fixed, angle theta1 at observation 1 gives distance d1 = h / tan(theta1), and angle theta2 (different from theta1, since the distance has changed) at observation 2 gives d2 = h / tan(theta2). The distance travelled between the two observations = the larger of d1, d2 minus the smaller. If the two observations are separated by a known time interval at a uniform speed, speed = distance travelled / time interval, which can then be used to find the time for any further remaining distance.
concepts.example: A 1.5 m tall boy walks towards a 30 m building; the angle of elevation of its top (28.5 m above his eyes) increases from 30 degrees to 60 degrees, giving horizontal distances of 28.5 root 3 m and 9.5 root 3 m, so he walked 19 root 3 m (Exercise 9.1, Q6, p. 141). A car's angle of depression from a tower changes from 30 degrees to 60 degrees six seconds later; the tower's height cancels out of the final calculation, giving 3 seconds for the car to reach the foot of the tower (Exercise 9.1, Q15, pp. 142-143).

questions.q: A fixed-height object is viewed from two different positions at two different angles of elevation. What stays the same in both right triangles?
questions.a: the height of the object
o: the length of the line of sight

questions.q: If the angle of elevation to a fixed-height object INCREASES as an observer walks towards it, the horizontal distance to the object
questions.a: decreases

questions.q: If d1 is the horizontal distance at the first observation and d2 is the horizontal distance at the second (with d1 greater than d2), the distance travelled between the two observations is d1 minus ____.
questions.a: d2

questions.q: A car is observed from the top of a tower at two different times as it approaches the tower's foot along a straight road. Which of the following is NOT a correct step in finding the time taken to travel between the two observation points?
questions.a: Add the two horizontal distances together, since the car's two positions are like two objects on opposite sides of the tower's foot
o: Add the two horizontal distances together, since the car's two positions are like two objects on opposite sides of the tower's foot
Find the two horizontal distances separately, using the tower's height with each angle of depression
Subtract the smaller (later) distance from the larger (earlier) distance to get the distance covered between the two observations
Divide the distance covered by the time interval between the two observations to get the car's uniform speed

questions.q: A balloon stays at a fixed height as the wind carries it horizontally away from an observer. As it moves farther away, the angle of elevation from the observer's eyes
questions.a: decreases

questions.q: A boy walks towards a tall building, keeping his eyes on its top. As he gets closer, the angle of elevation of the building's top
questions.a: increases

questions.q: In a two-position problem, why is the SAME height used in both right triangles, one for each observation?
questions.a: Because the object being viewed (the building, balloon or tower) does not change height between the two observations, only the observer's or the object's horizontal position changes
o: Because the object being viewed (the building, balloon or tower) does not change height between the two observations, only the observer's or the object's horizontal position changes
Because the two angles of elevation are always equal
Because trigonometric ratios cannot use two different heights
Because the horizontal distance never changes in these problems

questions.q: A car travels towards the foot of a tower along a straight road. Its angle of depression, seen from the top of the tower, is first 30 degrees, then later 60 degrees. Which observation corresponds to the car being closer to the tower?
questions.a: The 60-degree observation, since a larger angle of depression means a smaller horizontal distance
o: The 60-degree observation, since a larger angle of depression means a smaller horizontal distance
The 30-degree observation, since a smaller angle means the car has less distance left
Both observations are at the same distance
It cannot be determined from the angles alone

questions.q: A kite stays at a fixed height of 20 root 3 m. At one moment its angle of elevation from an observer is 30 degrees; a little later, having drifted further away, its angle of elevation is measured again. State, without calculating, whether this new angle is more or less than 30 degrees, and find the horizontal distance at the FIRST moment.
questions.a: Since the kite has drifted farther away, the horizontal distance has increased, so the new angle of elevation must be LESS than 30 degrees. At the first moment: tan 30 degrees = 20 root 3/d1, so 1/root 3 = 20 root 3/d1, giving d1 = 20 root 3 x root 3 = 60 m.
s: States correctly that the new angle is less than 30 degrees, with a valid reason
Correctly computes d1 = 60 m

questions.q: A tower is 30 m high. From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation of its top is 45 degrees. The horizontal distance from this point to the foot of the tower is
The same 30 m tower is observed from a second, closer point, where the angle of elevation is 60 degrees. The horizontal distance from this second point is ____ m (as a surd in simplest form).
questions.a: 10 root 3

questions.q: Continuing (30 m tower, distances 30 m at 45 degrees and 10 root 3 m at 60 degrees), the distance between the two observation points is
questions.a: 30 - 10 root 3 m (about 12.68 m)

questions.q: A building is 24 root 3 m high. From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation of its top is 30 degrees. Find the horizontal distance of this point from the foot of the building.
questions.a: tan 30 degrees = 24 root 3/d, so 1/root 3 = 24 root 3/d, giving d = 24 root 3 x root 3 = 72 m.
s: Sets up tan 30 degrees = 24 root 3/d correctly
Solves to get d = 72 m

questions.q: A building is 24 root 3 m high. An observer standing at a horizontal distance of 72 m (where the angle of elevation of its top is 30 degrees) walks towards the building until the angle of elevation becomes 60 degrees. Find the new horizontal distance, and hence the distance she walked.
questions.a: tan 60 degrees = 24 root 3/d2, so root 3 = 24 root 3/d2, giving d2 = 24 root 3/root 3 = 24 m. Distance walked = 72 - 24 = 48 m.
s: Correctly finds the new distance d2 = 24 m
Correctly finds the distance walked = 48 m

questions.q: A balloon stays at a fixed height of 40 root 3 m above the ground. At one moment, an observer on the ground measures its angle of elevation as 60 degrees. A little later, the wind has carried the balloon further away (still at the same height), and its angle of elevation is now 30 degrees. (i) Find the horizontal distance to the balloon at the first moment. (ii) Find the horizontal distance at the second moment. (iii) Find the distance travelled by the balloon.
questions.a: (i) tan 60 degrees = 40 root 3/d1, so d1 = 40 root 3/root 3 = 40 m. (ii) tan 30 degrees = 40 root 3/d2, so d2 = 40 root 3 x root 3 = 120 m. (iii) Distance travelled = d2 - d1 = 120 - 40 = 80 m.
s: Correctly finds d1 = 40 m at 60 degrees
Correctly finds d2 = 120 m at 30 degrees
Correctly subtracts to get the distance travelled = 80 m

questions.q: Assertion (A): A car approaches the foot of a tower along a straight road; the angle of depression from the top of the tower increases from 30 degrees to 60 degrees between two observations. The horizontal distance to the car is smaller at the second (60-degree) observation than at the first. Reason (R): For a fixed height, a larger angle of depression (or elevation) corresponds to a smaller horizontal distance, since the tangent of the angle increases as the horizontal distance decreases.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Consider these statements about a car observed from the top of a tower at two different times as it approaches along a straight road. (I) If the time interval between the two observations is known, along with the two horizontal distances, the car's average speed over that interval can be found. (II) The tower's own height must be known numerically before the time taken for the remaining distance to the foot of the tower can be found, since the height cannot be eliminated from the calculation. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: A man standing at the top of a tower observes a car on a straight road leading to the foot of the tower, at an angle of depression of 30 degrees. Six seconds later, at the same uniform speed, the car's angle of depression is found to be 60 degrees. (i) Letting the tower's height be h, express the horizontal distance to the car at each observation in terms of h. (ii) Find, in terms of h, the distance the car covered in those 6 seconds, and hence its speed. (iii) Find the time the car will take to travel from the second observation point to the foot of the tower, and show that your answer does not actually depend on h.
questions.a: (i) At 30 degrees: tan 30 degrees = h/d1, so d1 = h root 3. At 60 degrees: tan 60 degrees = h/d2, so d2 = h/root 3. (ii) Distance covered in 6 seconds = d1 - d2 = h root 3 - h/root 3 = h(3 - 1)/root 3 = 2h/root 3. Speed = distance/time = (2h/root 3)/6 = h/(3 root 3). (iii) Time for the remaining distance d2 = h/root 3 at this speed = d2 / speed = (h/root 3) divided by (h/(3 root 3)) = 3 seconds. The h cancels out completely in this last division, so the answer (3 seconds) does not depend on the actual height of the tower.
s: Correctly expresses d1 = h root 3 and d2 = h/root 3
Correctly finds the distance covered in 6 seconds and the speed in terms of h
Correctly finds the remaining time = 3 seconds and explicitly notes that h cancels out

questions.q: A classmate says: 'To find the time a car takes to reach the foot of a tower after the second observation, I must first find the actual height of the tower in metres.' Evaluate this claim, referring to what happens to the height h when the final time is calculated.
questions.a: The claim is false. Although the height h appears in both the distance-covered and the remaining-distance expressions, it cancels out completely when the remaining time is calculated as (remaining distance)/(speed), because both quantities are proportional to h. So the actual numerical height of the tower is never needed to answer this particular question.
s: States the claim is false
Explains that h cancels out because both the remaining distance and the speed are proportional to h

questions.q: Construct your own 'two observation' problem: choose a fixed height for an object (as a surd involving root 3, so that both distances come out as whole numbers) and two angles from 30, 45 and 60 degrees, so that the angle increases between the first and second observation. State your chosen values, and find the distance between the two observation points.
questions.a: Sample: height = 18 root 3 m. First angle of elevation = 30 degrees: tan 30 degrees = 18 root 3/d1, so d1 = 18 root 3 x root 3 = 54 m. Second angle of elevation = 60 degrees: tan 60 degrees = 18 root 3/d2, so d2 = 18 root 3/root 3 = 18 m. Distance between the two observation points = 54 - 18 = 36 m. (Any correctly worked height and pair of increasing angles from 30, 45 or 60 degrees is acceptable.)
s: Chooses a valid height (as a multiple of root 3) and two angles from 30, 45 or 60 degrees, with the angle increasing
Correctly finds both horizontal distances for the chosen values
Correctly subtracts to get the distance between the two observation points
